source.title: Robust Testing for Deep Learning using Human Label Noise
source.authors: Gordon Lim; Stefan Larson; Kevin Leach

record.tranche_reason: The study measures memorization of human and synthetic noisy labels and reports that some incorrect human labels are learned without memorization, refining the claim about how noisy labels are learned. It does not test training order or fitting completely random labels.
record.gate_note: The study's memorization results bear on noisy-label learning, but do not test fitting completely random labels or the order in which real and noisy labels are learned. Figure 1 and Figure 2 findings are described qualitatively in the text; exact plotted values are not stated.
record.test_reason: The study invokes real-patterns-first learning to motivate noisy-label methods, but measures example-level inclusion/exclusion probabilities and robustness to feature-dependent noise. It reports neither learning order nor complete random-label fitting. These results do not test V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: some incorrect human labels are learned without dependence on individual-example inclusion and form subclusters in CLIP feature space. CBN reduces tested methods' accuracy relative to PMD, while SNLS improves LRA-Diffusion performance. The authors do not establish when noisy labels are learned.
record.recipe_differences: The study estimates example-level memorization through a subsampling estimator and analyzes human versus synthetic noisy labels; it does not reproduce the random-label fitting experiments or measure training dynamics from the cited studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis uses CIFAR-10N Random 1, selected because it produced the largest reported performance drop among the Random sets; the heldout analysis uses labels whose inclusion and exclusion probabilities both exceed 0.6 for the focused human-label subset.

fits_no_version.finding: Some incorrect human labels have high inclusion and exclusion probabilities, with greater density in this region than synthetic class-dependent incorrect labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature-dependent human labeling errors can be predicted from other training examples without memorizing the individual example.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic incorrect labels more often have low memorization scores, but separating inclusion and exclusion probabilities shows that low scores can reflect failure to learn either with or without the example.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low inclusion-based memorization scores alone do not distinguish generalizable label patterns from unlearned labels.

record.peer_reviewed: Workshop on Deep Learning for Testing and Testing for Deep Learning
record.problems: The memorization distributions are reported qualitatively in figures without exact values in the text. The analysis estimates memorization only for a heldout subset and selects CIFAR-10N Random 1; it does not measure training order or random-label fitting.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steady test-error degradation across the full random-corruption range. Table I reports only test accuracy at two feature-dependent noise levels.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms clean-label generalization.
Whether real patterns precede noisy-label memorization and how real and random labels are learned over training.

record.verdict_notes: CIFAR-10N Random 1 selects among human annotations; it is not a completely random labeling of CIFAR-10. The study's memorization definition measures sensitivity to example inclusion, not learning chronology.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random labels with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, and their test error.
Training time and convergence speed as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled, permuted, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training fit and test error across corruption levels.
Effects of explicit regularization, its removal, and generalization on true labels.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, and how learning changes over training.

rows.subject: ResNet34 models (1,500 models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated memorization values for heldout incorrect human noisy labels using subsampling.

conditions.value: subset; equal number of incorrect and correct labels
30% of heldout set excluded per model

rows.value: The text says incorrect human noisy labels include a greater proportion of high memorization scores than incorrect synthetic labels; exact values not stated.
rows.note: Figure 1 is described qualitatively; no exact distribution values are stated.
rows.check: The qualitative histogram comparison is supported, but this memorization score does not measure training dynamics or complete random-label fitting. High scores indicate dependence on example inclusion, not when labels were learned.

rows.subject: ResNet34 models (1,500 models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated memorization values for heldout incorrect synthetic class-dependent noisy labels using subsampling.

conditions.value: subset; equal number of incorrect and correct labels
30% of heldout set excluded per model

rows.value: The text says incorrect synthetic noisy labels show a greater proportion of low memorization scores than incorrect human noisy labels; exact values not stated.
rows.note: Figure 1 is described qualitatively; no exact distribution values are stated.
rows.check: The qualitative comparison is supported. Low memorization scores can reflect labels that were never learned, so they cannot establish learning without memorization or bear on V6.

rows.subject: ResNet34 models (1,500 models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated inclusion and exclusion probabilities for heldout incorrect human noisy labels.

conditions.value: inclusion and exclusion probabilities both exceed 0.6

rows.measure: Density of examples with high inclusion and exclusion probabilities
rows.value: The text reports a greater density of incorrect human noisy labels in the top-right region; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The text describes a greater density but does not give counts or a numeric effect size.
rows.check: High inclusion and exclusion probabilities support prediction of some incorrect human labels without their inclusion in training. They do not establish learning order. The 0.6 threshold defines the subset selected for subsequent feature analysis.

rows.subject: ResNet34 models (1,500 models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated inclusion and exclusion probabilities for heldout incorrect synthetic class-dependent noisy labels.
rows.measure: Density of examples with high inclusion and exclusion probabilities
rows.value: The text says synthetic incorrect labels tend to be sparse in the top-right region; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The text describes the distribution qualitatively; no exact values are stated.
rows.check: The qualitative sparsity comparison is supported, but it measures dependence on example inclusion rather than any version's training-fit or temporal effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
